lesson.title: Making Sense of the Numbers: From Data to Conclusions
lesson.summary: Data interpretation is the process of drawing sound conclusions from experimental results by looking at trends, variability, and the size of differences between groups rather than just comparing raw averages.
lesson.body:
Collecting data is only half of any experiment, the other half is figuring out what the data actually mean. A controlled experiment is designed to isolate the effect of one independent variable on a dependent variable while holding other conditions constant, but even a well designed experiment produces numbers that need careful interpretation before they support any conclusion. Two treatment groups almost never come out with identical averages just by chance, so the central question in data interpretation is usually not whether two averages differ, since they almost always do at least slightly, but whether that difference is meaningful or just reflects ordinary variability.

This is exactly where standard deviation becomes a tool for interpretation rather than just a descriptive statistic. Suppose one group of plants grown under a control condition has a mean height of 14 cm with a standard deviation of about 3.16 cm, the same numbers calculated in the previous chapter, and a second group grown under an experimental treatment has a mean height of 20 cm with a standard deviation of 2.5 cm. Simply comparing the two means, 14 cm versus 20 cm, might tempt a quick conclusion that the treatment increased height. But a responsible interpretation also considers the spread within each group: since the standard deviations are moderate relative to the six centimeter gap between the means, and the range of typical values in each group, roughly the mean plus or minus one standard deviation, does not overlap heavily, the difference looks more likely to reflect a real effect of the treatment than random noise. If the standard deviations had instead been very large, say 8 cm in each group, the same six centimeter gap between means would look much less convincing, since individual measurements from the two groups would overlap substantially.

A rigorous interpretation does not stop at eyeballing the overlap, which is why the chi-square test from an earlier chapter, and other formal statistical tests built on similar logic, exist to put a precise probability on whether an observed difference is likely due to chance. Data interpretation also means staying alert to patterns that are easy to over-read: a correlation between two variables, such as two measurements that rise together across a data set, does not by itself prove that one causes the other, since both could be influenced by some third factor, or the relationship could run in a direction other than the one assumed. Outliers, individual data points that fall far outside the pattern of the rest of the data, deserve scrutiny too, since they might reflect a measurement error worth excluding or a genuinely interesting biological exception worth investigating further, and the interpreter has to make and justify that judgment rather than automatically discarding inconvenient numbers.

Good data interpretation ultimately connects back to the original hypothesis and experimental design. A conclusion is only as strong as the design that produced the data: if the independent variable was properly controlled and the dependent variable was measured consistently, and the difference between groups is large relative to the variability within each group, then the data provide meaningful support for a real biological effect. If any of those conditions is shaky, the appropriate conclusion is caution rather than certainty, and often a call for a repeated or larger experiment. The next chapter turns these same ideas into a visual form, since a well built graph is often the fastest way to communicate exactly this kind of comparison between means, spread, and overlap.
